entries.name: Sequential Model-based Algorithm Configuration
entries.definition: A sequential algorithm-configuration procedure that uses random-forest performance models to propose parameter settings and compares candidate settings with an incumbent through adaptive evaluations on shared problem instances and random seeds.
entries.identity_notes: The primary scope is the original 2011 SMAC procedure, not every sequential model-based optimizer or every later SMAC software release. It configures a target algorithm over a set or distribution of instances and returns one incumbent configuration; it is not per-instance algorithm selection, a prediction forest by itself, or population-based transfer of trained model weights. Its model-guided proposals distinguish it from ROAR, which shares the intensification procedure but samples configurations at random. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 262 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktree and main checkout, returning 9 lines in each checkout. These were prior candidate leads, source references and neighboring-method mentions, not existing records for these identities. Ten exact AIO CLASS nodes with synonyms and outgoing edges and eight neighboring native mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The original method explicitly lacks adaptive capping of individual poor runs. Its adaptive allocation of additional evaluations must not be equated with the censored-runtime handling or other features of later SMAC releases.

Surrogate uncertainty and early empirical comparisons do not certify an optimal configuration or generalization to unseen instance distributions. The paper’s asymptotic argument assumes a finite configuration space, consistent cost estimates and unbounded evaluation growth; the displayed experimental procedure caps incumbent evaluations with maxR=2000. These conditions are not an unconditional guarantee for the capped implementation or continuous spaces.

Instance features are optional; the result is a single configuration and does not require test-instance feature computation. The reviewed source is an author-hosted manuscript, not a claim that its 15 PDF pages match the publisher’s page layout. No benchmark result or executable implementation was reproduced.

claims.statement: Initialize with an evaluation of the default configuration, or a random setting when no default is available. Fit a random-forest surrogate using configuration values and, when available, training-instance features. Aggregate each tree’s predictions over instances according to the chosen cost metric, then derive predictive moments across trees. For runtime optimization the paper uses log-transformed responses while preserving the original aggregation objective through inverse transformation at leaves. Rank proposals by expected improvement, using its log-cost formulation, and search for promising settings with multistart one-coordinate local changes plus randomly sampled acquisition candidates. Interleave guided proposals with uniformly sampled configurations. The intensification routine compares a challenger and incumbent on shared instance/seed evaluations, enlarges the challenger’s evaluated subset in doubling batches, rejects it when its empirical cost is worse, and replaces the incumbent when the challenger has matched the available evaluation set and is at least as good. Repeat model fitting and configuration comparisons within the overall configuration budget.

entries.name: FABOLAS
entries.definition: A Bayesian hyperparameter optimization algorithm that jointly chooses a model configuration and training-data subset size using surrogate models of loss and evaluation cost, directing evaluations toward information about the best configuration on the full dataset.
entries.identity_notes: FABOLAS treats dataset size as an environmental evaluation variable while retaining the full dataset as the optimization target. It differs from Gaussian-process regression alone, fixed-fidelity Bayesian optimization, a discrete multi-task optimizer with manually selected task sizes, and Hyperband’s predetermined resource brackets. The paper method and the separately pinned RoBO implementation are recorded as distinct source versions. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 262 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktree and main checkout, returning 9 lines in each checkout. These were prior candidate leads, source references and neighboring-method mentions, not existing records for these identities. Ten exact AIO CLASS nodes with synonyms and outgoing edges and eight neighboring native mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: Extrapolation depends on the adequacy of the loss-versus-size and cost models. Small subsets need not preserve the ranking at full size, and the returned projected incumbent need not have a confirming full-data evaluation or optimal test performance.

The paper’s loss basis (1,(1-s)^2) allows a monotonic latent trend at fixed configuration but does not by itself force that trend to decrease when coefficient signs are unconstrained. Its polynomial-cost interpretation also depends on the size coordinate: log-cost affine in raw relative size is exponential in that coordinate; the pinned code instead uses normalized log dataset counts.

The pinned code logs both objective and cost, applies Latin-hypercube initialization and a RandomSampling acquisition optimizer, and leaves the acquisition overhead at zero through the inspected call chain. Those choices are not silently attributed to the paper’s algorithm. Positive objective/cost values and compatible parameter settings are required by that source; static inspection is not a runtime result.

No universal speedup, exact information-gain computation or independent calibration result is asserted. The full entropy-search implementation and the paper’s supplementary experiments were not audited.

claims.statement: Model loss and computational cost as functions of configuration and dataset fraction, using Gaussian-process surrogates with a kernel over configuration coordinates and a finite-rank basis over size. Begin with evaluations of configurations on small subsets. Select the next configuration/size pair using an entropy-search acquisition focused on the minimizer at full dataset size; the paper divides its information criterion by predicted evaluation cost plus optimization overhead. Evaluate the selected pair, observe loss and cost, and update the models. Select the incumbent among configurations already evaluated by projecting their predicted loss to the full dataset, rather than requiring each candidate to have been evaluated there. The paper integrates surrogate hyperparameters using MCMC and describes DIRECT/CMA-ES acquisition optimization; the inspected code has separate implementation choices.

claims.statement: In the inspected RoBO revision, dataset counts are mapped to a normalized log2 coordinate between the selected minimum and maximum; proposed coordinates are transformed back and rounded to integer counts. Quadratic loss and linear cost basis functions operate on that transformed coordinate, while both observed objective values and costs are logged. The outer function uses a Latin-hypercube initial design and RandomSampling acquisition maximizer. Its marginalized acquisition update passes no overhead keyword, so the per-unit-cost estimator sets overhead to zero and divides by the exponentiated predicted log-cost mean. These are static observations of this revision, not claims of equality with the original experiments or executable compatibility.

entries.name: DEHB
entries.definition: A hyperparameter optimization algorithm that combines Hyperband resource schedules with differential-evolution populations at different resource levels, using promising lower-resource configurations to guide proposals evaluated and selected at higher resource levels.
entries.identity_notes: DEHB is the combined resource-allocation and differential-evolution method, distinct from generic genetic algorithms, differential evolution alone, random-proposal Hyperband, KDE-guided BOHB and ASHA’s asynchronous within-stage promotions. Budget-specific populations contain configuration vectors, not a population of trained checkpoints whose weights are copied between configurations. The proceedings paper and the versioned appendix are distinguished explicitly. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 262 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktree and main checkout, returning 9 lines in each checkout. These were prior candidate leads, source references and neighboring-method mentions, not existing records for these identities. Ten exact AIO CLASS nodes with synonyms and outgoing edges and eight neighboring native mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The source’s initialization prose and pseudocode use bracket and iteration terminology inconsistently. Algorithm3’s bracket_counter==0 condition spans an outer cycle and applies direct promotion only for i>0. The record describes the common mechanism without treating every printed initialization statement as byte-equivalent executable steps.

Appendix Algorithm2 prints b0=(bmax/bmin)*eta^(-s), which gives normalized rather than absolute budgets when bmin differs from1. Its return order for counts and budgets is reversed at the Algorithm3 call site. These discrepancies are retained as source qualifications; no author-issued erratum or exact executable schedule is claimed.

The appendix updates its incumbent after evaluations without an explicit full-budget restriction. The record therefore does not promise that the returned best observed configuration has been verified at maximum resource. Greedy same-budget replacement limits harmful transfers but is not a proof of global optimality or universal robustness.

Continuous encodings impose numerical neighborhoods on categorical choices, and low-fidelity information can be misleading. Parallel completion order can affect shared populations. No benchmark speedup, constant total runtime or author-code execution is claimed.

claims.statement: Maintain a differential-evolution subpopulation for each Hyperband resource level, sized according to the maximum number of evaluations assigned to that level. Iterate through the prescribed halving brackets. For a bracket’s starting level use evolution within its own population; for higher levels form a parent pool from promising lower-level configurations and use it for difference-vector mutation, followed by crossover with a target in the current level’s population. Evaluate the proposed configuration at the current level and retain it only according to a same-level fitness comparison with the target. Supplement an undersized mutation pool from a global pool of configurations. The initialization cycle includes direct lower-to-higher promotions before the general evolutionary transfer pattern. For mixed search spaces, the appendix keeps continuous population coordinates in a unit hypercube and maps copies to numerical or binned ordinal/categorical settings for evaluation. Its parallel design keeps each halving stage synchronized while allowing brackets to overlap and applying completed differential-evolution updates immediately.

native_neighbors.name: Hyperband
native_neighbors.definition: A hyperparameter resource-allocation algorithm that runs successive-halving brackets with different initial configuration counts and starting budgets, balancing broad early screening against more conservative evaluation.

claims.statement: Choose a maximum per-configuration resource R and reduction factor eta. In the finite-horizon Algorithm1, set s_max=floor(log_eta(R)) and B=(s_max+1)*R. For each bracket s from s_max down to zero, start with n=ceil((B/R)*eta^s/(s+1)) configurations and r=R*eta^(−s) resource units. Evaluate current candidates at geometrically increasing resource levels and retain the best approximately 1/eta fraction after each comparison. The s=0 bracket evaluates its candidates directly at R. Algorithm1 returns the configuration with the smallest intermediate loss observed, rather than specifying selection only among maximum-budget evaluations. Brackets address uncertainty about how many configurations to start and how long to evaluate before elimination. Resources can denote iterations, time, data or features; actual computational cost and whether work can be resumed depend on that choice.

claims.statement: Keep observations separated by evaluation budget. For proposals, use the highest budget with enough data to build better- and worse-performing configuration densities. Retain a positive fraction of random configurations, and fall back to random sampling when no model is available. Hyperband brackets and successive halving then allocate increasing resources to surviving candidates. Observations are shared across brackets, but the proposal density is not fitted by pooling all fidelity levels indiscriminately. The method can schedule multiple brackets and concurrent evaluations; the paper’s worker policy favors waiting smaller-budget jobs. native_neighbors.name: Tree-structured Parzen Estimator
native_neighbors.definition: A sequential hyperparameter optimization method that separates observations by a loss quantile, fits tree-structured densities for the better and remaining configurations, and proposes evaluations using their density ratio as an expected-improvement ranking.

claims.statement: Represent valid configurations with a conditional generative tree so that some variables are active only for particular parent choices. Given observed configurations and losses to minimize, choose a loss threshold at a quantile gamma and fit l(x) from observations below that threshold and g(x) from the remainder. The model uses p(x|y)=l(x) below the threshold and g(x) otherwise, with p(x)=gamma*l(x)+(1−gamma)*g(x). Under this construction, expected nonnegative improvement E[max(y*−y,0)] is proportional, across configurations, to [gamma+(1−gamma)*g(x)/l(x)]^−1 wherever the relevant densities and expectation are defined. Draw candidate configurations from l, rank them by this expression, evaluate the selected candidate’s actual loss, and incorporate the observation into subsequent density estimates. The original estimator replaces continuous priors with adaptive Parzen mixtures around observed values and retains a prior component; bounded uniform variables use truncated Gaussian mixtures, log-uniform variables are modeled in log space, and categorical probabilities are reweighted by observed counts. The tree specifies conditional variable activation, not a decision tree that predicts loss. This is distinct from the separate Gaussian-process surrogate described in Section 3 of the same paper.

native_neighbors.definition: A population-based neural-network training procedure that interleaves parameter updates with performance-guided copying of partially trained models and exploration of hyperparameters, producing training trajectories with changing hyperparameter settings.

claims.statement: Maintain population members with model parameters, hyperparameters, an evaluation score and training progress. Each worker trains its parameters with its current hyperparameters and evaluates a chosen performance metric, which need not be differentiable or identical to the local training objective. When a readiness condition holds, an exploitation rule can replace that worker’s parameters and hyperparameters with those of another promising member. An exploration rule then perturbs or resamples the copied hyperparameters, and training continues from the inherited weights. Algorithm 1 calls exploration and re-evaluation only when exploitation changes the weights; its final output is the population member’s parameters with the highest recorded score. Readiness, selection and mutation rules depend on the application. The original procedure is asynchronous: members need access to population scores, parameters and hyperparameters, but no population-wide synchronization barrier is required. Alternating local parameter learning with slower model selection and hyperparameter changes yields schedules along training lineages, rather than restricting each run to one fixed hyperparameter configuration.

evidence.locator: Section 3, Equations (1)–(4) and Algorithm 1, PDF pp. 4–6; identity and related work on pp. 1–4

aio_mappings.rationale: PBT organizes model training through parameter inheritance and hyperparameter adaptation. The pinned target is a broad training-strategy concept described as preprocessing; the relation connects these scopes without treating this iterative optimizer as preprocessing or asserting an is-a relationship.

limitations: The original algorithm specifies application-dependent readiness, exploitation and exploration. PBA’s quartile selection, three-epoch interval, operation probabilities and schedule-only transfer are not general PBT requirements.
Asynchrony removes a global training barrier but does not remove the need to exchange model state and performance information. Reusing weights is not weight averaging or an inference-time ensemble.

Score-driven selection depends on the evaluation protocol, search space, budget and population behavior. The record asserts no global optimum, universal cost equivalence, wall-clock speedup or generalization guarantee.

native_neighbors.name: Asynchronous Successive Halving
native_neighbors.definition: An asynchronous resource-allocation algorithm that promotes promising completed hyperparameter trials through increasing resource levels as workers become available and starts new trials when no eligible promotion is available, without waiting for an entire evaluation stage to finish.

claims.statement: Choose minimum and maximum resources r and R, a reduction factor eta, and starting-level offset s. Resource at rung k is r*eta^(s+k). Dispatch work to free workers and record completed rung losses. In the author dissertation’s Algorithm 3, scan promotable rungs from the highest eligible level downward, stopping below the maximum-resource rung. At each level, consider the currently best approximately 1/eta fraction of completed configurations and select an eligible one that has not already been promoted. If the entire scan yields none, sample a new configuration for the base rung. Thus the starting cohort can grow and promotions do not wait for every job at a rung. Promoted configurations may later fall outside the hindsight top fraction as additional results arrive. Checkpointing can reuse a trial’s previous training; it is distinct from copying weights between different configurations. The maximum resource limits promotion depth in this bounded version.

evidence.locator: Sections 3.1–3.3 and Algorithms 1–2, PDF pp.3–5; Algorithm 2 indentation qualified using the author dissertation
Section 3.3.2 and Algorithm 3, PDF pp.72–74 (printed 59–61), especially get_job lines13–21 on PDF p.73/printed 60
